tagline.text: A hillside neighborhood in La Trinidad painted with sunflowers and rainbows

location.label: Location
location.text: Barangay Balili, La Trinidad, Benguet (sitios Stonehill, Botiwtiw and Sadjap), beside the Baguio–La Trinidad road

best_season.label: Best time to visit
best_season.text: November–April dry season (mornings on clear days recommended)

budget.label: Budget
budget.text: About ₱50–500 (round-trip transport and snacks from Baguio, per person)

airport.label: Nearest airport
airport.text: Ninoy Aquino International Airport (MNL), about 5–6 hours overland; Loakan Airport in Baguio is another option

children.text: StoBoSa is a large community mural that paints roughly 150–200 hillside homes in La Trinidad, Benguet, in bright colors. Unveiled in 2016 and described as the first and one of the largest community artworks in the Philippines, it is about a 10-minute jeepney ride from Baguio and easy to fit into a half-day plan.

StoBoSa is a name made from the first syllables of three neighborhoods in Barangay Balili, La Trinidad: Stonehill, Botiwtiw and Sadjap. Its official name is the StoBoSa Hillside Homes Artwork. According to Wikipedia, the site lies at about 16.4344°N, 120.5976°E, and the La Trinidad municipal government has officially designated it a tourist attraction. Head a short way north of central Baguio and the hillside on the right side of the road is covered in colorful houses, so even first-time visitors recognize it right away.

The mural was conceived by the Department of Tourism's Cordillera office (DOT-CAR) and the La Trinidad local government as part of the Rev-Bloom Urban Redevelopment Tourism Campaign. The design was done by artists of the Chanum Foundation, linked to the Tam-awan Village artists' community, and Wikipedia says the group was led by Jordan Mang-osan. Resident training began in January 2016, painting started in February, and a public unveiling was held on June 23 of the same year. The work was about 80 percent complete then, with completion targeted for around August. About 520 people took part, including residents of the three neighborhoods and volunteers.

The design draws on the favela murals of Rio de Janeiro in Brazil, and some media say it was also inspired by Gamcheon Culture Village in Busan, Korea. Each house looks like an ordinary wall up close, but from a distance the whole slope reads as one large picture, with the sunflower as its main motif. The sunflowers are said to honor the area's past as a place full of flowers. Rainbow patterns also appear here and there. The project covers more than 18,000 square meters and reportedly used about 2,800 gallons of paint costing around ₱2 million, supplied by the local paint company Davies Paints.

Because paint fades over time, the mural has been touched up more than once. SunStar reported that on April 26, 2019, the Department of Tourism, the La Trinidad mayor and the community coordinator Gloria Agasen held a repainting event with around 150 participants. The same article says the local government had installed a new view deck and planned to improve the hanging bridge and restrooms. The view deck is known to have been pursued since 2016, when the La Trinidad council was reported to be allotting about ₱1.6 million for it together with parking. Local media reported in 2023 that a project to repaint about 300 houses in a new design was under way. The colors and progress today may differ, so check recent photos or local news before you go.

The walls and roofs of the houses were painted so that together they form one sunflower pattern. It is hard to recognize up close and only shows its full shape from across the road or farther away, so step back to take it in.
Bold, favela-inspired colors run along the slope. Blue, yellow, orange and green photograph at their sharpest in clear sunlight, while on cloudy days the colors can look muted.

A 2019 report says the local government built a new view deck. It is a good spot to take in the whole mural, but its location and whether it is open may vary over time, so follow the on-site instructions.

blocks.title: A real neighborhood where people live

children.text: This is a residential area, not an exhibition hall. Daily life goes on in every house even after the designation as a tourist site, so walk quietly through the lanes and do not photograph the insides of homes.

The Chanum Foundation and artists from Tam-awan Village handled the design. Wikipedia lists Niño Jose Seriosa, Ged Alangui, Clinton Aniversario and Jenny Lorenzo among the contributors. Pairing this stop with Tam-awan Village in Baguio helps you understand the character of Cordillera art.

It sits right beside the road linking Baguio and La Trinidad, so you can see it the moment you step off the jeepney. The low effort required makes it easy to slot into spare time during a Baguio trip.
Local media reported that the original design is kept while a "waves of colors" design and works by local artists are added. The look may change slightly from visit to visit.
Around the La Trinidad market you can browse highland produce such as vegetables and strawberries. Strawberry seasons and prices change every year, so check locally.

items.title: Half-day route
items.subtitle: From Baguio to StoBoSa and a strawberry farm

children.text: Take a La Trinidad–bound jeepney from the Session Road or Magsaysay Avenue area in central Baguio. The ride to StoBoSa takes about
10 minutes
, and it helps to tell the conductor in advance that you want to get off at StoBoSa.
From a safe spot across the road, first photograph the whole mural. The colors look sharpest when morning light falls on the neighborhood.
Go up to the view deck or along the lanes in the village to see the mural up close. Keep your voice down, since this is a residential area, and do not block the middle of the path.
Return to the road and take a La Trinidad–bound jeepney or taxi to a strawberry farm or the market.
Have lunch in La Trinidad, then return to Baguio. Catch the jeepney back from the opposite side of the road.
The times are examples and vary with traffic and weather.

items.title: Baguio combination route
items.subtitle: Together with Baguio sights in one day

children.text: Look around Burnham Park or Session Road in Baguio first, then head to StoBoSa later in the morning.
Eat in La Trinidad and visit a strawberry farm.
Return to Baguio and continue to city sights such as Mines View Park or Wright Park. If the weather is cloudy and the light fades early, move your outdoor plans earlier.
The bus from Manila to Baguio usually takes 5–6 hours. Several companies run long-distance buses from terminals such as Pasay, so check the latest timetables.
From Baguio you continue to StoBoSa by jeepney. A day trip from Manila is long and tiring, so staying one night in Baguio is recommended.
Bus fares and timetables change with the season, so confirm them before you leave.
In central Baguio, take a jeepney bound for Acop, Tomay, Buyagan or La Trinidad. Many board near Session Road or Magsaysay Avenue.
StoBoSa is about
3km
from the city center (KM 3), a ride of about
10 minutes
. The mural is visible on the right side of the road.
Since 28 September 2026 the minimum traditional jeepney fare (first 4 km) is ₱14 (₱17 for modern jeepneys), and 2026 travel guides put the Baguio–La Trinidad fare at about
. The ₱9 in older blogs is out of date, so confirm the fare with the driver when you board.
Going by taxi from central Baguio, the cost varies with traffic. Confirm whether the meter will be used before you board.
On the way back, take a Baguio-bound jeepney from the opposite side of the road. Jeepneys run along this road, so you do not need to book a taxi separately.

Baguio and the Benguet highlands sit at high elevation and are cooler than most of the Philippines. The dry season from November to April has many clear days, which suits photographing the mural's colors. In the morning especially, the mist often lifts and the whole village stands out sharply.

In the rainy season from June to October, rain and mist reduce visibility and make the slope lanes slippery. When a typhoon approaches, road conditions worsen, so check the weather forecast. In February the Panagbenga flower festival takes place in Baguio and the area gets very crowded. Check the festival schedule each year.

No large dining district right in front of StoBoSa has been confirmed, so most visitors eat and stay in central Baguio or central La Trinidad. In Baguio, lodging and restaurants cluster around Session Road, and as befits a highland city, hot soups suit the cool weather. Specific businesses change over time, so check recent ratings before choosing.

La Trinidad is well known as the "strawberry capital," and neighboring villages grow many vegetables. Visitors are said to be able to pick strawberries at farms or try strawberry jam and strawberry desserts. Strawberries may be out of season, so check when you plan to visit.

StoBoSa alone takes about an hour, so it works well combined with a Baguio itinerary, in the morning or late afternoon. It also helps to visit other local art spots in the Cordillera, such as Tam-awan Village, to understand the background of the artists who made the mural. Check location and opening hours locally.
Go on a sunny morning for the sharpest colors. On cloudy days it is better to go early rather than in the afternoon.
To see the whole mural, shoot from across the road or from farther away. Up close the sunflower pattern is hard to take in at a glance.
Keep your voice down and respect privacy, since this is a residential area. It is best to ask permission before photographing someone's home.
The slope is steep, so wear non-slip sneakers. It is especially slippery after rain.
Reports mention donations for the upkeep of the village, so it helps to carry a small amount.
Cars pass quickly along the roadside, so do not step into the road to take photos.
Baguio has a large day-night temperature gap, so bring a thin jacket.
The mural has been repainted, so checking recent photos or news before you go reduces disappointment.
This is a residential neighborhood close to a road. Walk quietly and do not take photos in the roadway.
Traffic along the roadside is heavy, so take care when crossing.
The slopes and steps are slippery, and some stretches may have no railings.
Keep your phone and wallet in front of you to guard against pickpockets.
No confirmed information exists on admission, opening hours or the state of the view deck, so follow local guidance.
Landslides and road closures can occur in the rainy and typhoon seasons, so check weather notices.
